d: Overview of Roblox's rigid body physics engine, assemblies, and constraints.
h:
Roblox uses a rigid body physics engine. BaseParts are subject to physical forces as long as they are not Anchored. You can create physical assemblies using attachments and constraints, and you can detect and control collisions between objects using events and collision filtering.

Assemblies

An assembly is one or more BaseParts connected by rigid constraints or motors (animated rigid joints). Assemblies can be set to an initial linear or angular velocity, or their behavior can be affected through constraints.

<img src="../assets/physics/assemblies/Assembly-Example-Block.png" alt="A light blue cube against a dark blue background that represents an assembly of 1 part." width="100%" />
<figcaption>1 assembly; 1 part</figcaption>

<img src="../assets/physics/assemblies/Assembly-Example-Avatar.png" alt="A humanoid character model against a dark blue background that represents an assembly of 18 parts." width="100%" />
<figcaption>1 assembly; 18 parts</figcaption>

<img src="../assets/physics/assemblies/Assembly-Example-Ship.png" alt="A pirate that represents an assemble of 179 parts." width="100%" />
<figcaption>1 assembly; 179 parts</figcaption>

Constraints

Non-anchored assemblies react to force from gravity and collisions, but physical force can also be applied and simulated through mechanical constraints or mover constraints.

Mechanical constraints include familiar objects like hinges, springs, and ropes which can be used to build mechanisms. Each is summarized in the mechanical constraints guide.

Mover constraints apply velocity, force, or torque to assemblies, align assemblies by position or orientation, and more. Each is summarized in the mover constraints guide.

Collisions

Collision events automatically occur when two BaseParts touch or stop touching in the 3D world. You can detect these collisions through the Touched and TouchEnded events which occur regardless of either part's CanCollide property value.

Through collision filtering techniques such as collision groups or part‑to‑part filtering, you can control which physical assemblies collide with others.

See the collisions guide for more details on detecting and filtering collisions.

Network ownership

In order to support complex physical mechanisms while also aiming for a smooth and responsive experience for players, the Roblox physics engine utilizes a distributed physics system in which computations are distributed between the server and all connected clients. Within this system, the engine assigns network ownership of physically simulated BaseParts to either a client or server to divide the work of calculating physics. See the network ownership guide for further details.

Adaptive timestepping

The engine emphasizes best performance by automatically assigning assemblies to one of three simulation rates. For scenarios featuring complex mechanisms like tanks, you can improve stability by setting a fixed timestep. See the adaptive timestepping guide for more information.

Sleep system

When an assembly is not moving or accelerating, the Roblox physics engine improves performance by automatically stops simulating the assembly. See the sleep system guide for details.

kid.simple: Roblox has a physics engine that makes unanchored parts fall, bounce, roll and crash into each other, a lot like real objects. This page is a map of all the physics topics: assemblies, constraints, collisions, network ownership, timestepping and the sleep system. Physics is what makes cars drive, doors swing and towers topple, so it is worth learning early.
kid.analogy: Think of the physics engine as an invisible referee that, many times every second, looks at every loose object and decides where it moves next: "you are falling, you just hit that wall, you are being pulled by a spring."
keyPoints: Roblox uses a rigid body physics engine, which means parts never bend or squish. They only move and spin as solid pieces.
Any part that is not anchored is affected by gravity and collisions. Anchored parts stay frozen in place.
An assembly is one or more parts stuck together that physics moves as a single object. A character is 1 assembly made of 18 parts.
Mechanical constraints (hinges, springs, ropes and more) connect parts to build machines. Mover constraints push, spin or line up assemblies.
The `Touched` and `TouchEnded` events fire when parts start or stop touching, even if `CanCollide` is off. Collision groups let you choose what can bump into what.
Network ownership splits physics work between the server and players' devices so movement feels smooth.
Roblox saves effort by running simple things at slower simulation rates (adaptive timestepping) and by pausing objects that are not moving (the sleep system).

terms.physics engine: The part of Roblox that calculates how objects move, fall and collide, many times every second.
terms.rigid body: A solid object that never bends or stretches. A rigid wooden plank in Roblox stays exactly the same shape even if a car lands on it.
terms.anchored: A part with `Anchored = true` is frozen in place. Gravity and hits cannot move it.
terms.assembly: A group of parts joined so they move as one object. 1 part alone is 1 assembly; a pirate ship of 179 welded parts can also be 1 assembly.
terms.linear velocity: How fast and in which direction something is moving, in studs per second. `Vector3.new(0, 10, 0)` means moving up at 10 studs every second.
terms.angular velocity: How fast something is spinning, and around which axis.
terms.force / torque: A force is a push or pull in a direction. A torque is a twist that makes something spin.
terms.constraint: A physics rule or connection between parts, like a hinge that only lets a door swing.
terms.collision: When two solid parts bump into each other and the engine stops them from overlapping.
terms.collision filtering: Choosing which objects can bump into each other. For example, players could walk through a team door while enemies cannot.
terms.network ownership: Which computer, the server or one player's device, is in charge of calculating a part's physics.
terms.timestep: The small slice of time between physics updates. Smaller steps are more accurate but cost more work.
terms.sleep: When an assembly stops moving, the engine pauses calculating it to save effort, and wakes it up when something touches it.

example.title: Drop a crate and watch it land
example.code:
local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local crate = Instance.new("Part")
crate.Size = Vector3.new(4, 4, 4)
crate.Position = Vector3.new(0, 50, 0)  -- start 50 studs up
crate.Anchored = false                   -- let physics move it
crate.Parent = Workspace

crate.Touched:Connect(function(otherPart)
	print("Crate hit", otherPart.Name)
end)

-- Default gravity is 196.2 studs per second squared
print("Gravity is", Workspace.Gravity)
explain: We make a 4-stud crate 50 studs in the air and leave it unanchored so the physics engine controls it.
Gravity pulls it down. With the default `Workspace.Gravity` of 196.2, after 0.5 seconds of falling it is already moving about 98 studs per second (196.2 x 0.5).
When it lands, `Touched` fires and prints the name of what it hit, such as `Baseplate`.

watchOut: If your part will not move, check `Anchored`. Anchored parts ignore gravity and forces completely.
If your build falls apart when you press Play, the pieces are not joined into one assembly. Weld them together or anchor the base.
`Touched` still fires when `CanCollide` is off, so a see-through trigger zone can still detect players.
